title: SEX WITH YOUR SPOUSE COULD MAKE BOTH OF YOU “UNCLEAN” UNTIL EVENING—SO WHY DID GOD SAY THAT?
paragraphs: SEX WITH YOUR SPOUSE COULD MAKE BOTH OF YOU “UNCLEAN” UNTIL EVENING—SO WHY DID GOD SAY THAT?

Leviticus 15 contains one of the Bible’s most misunderstood statements about sex—and when you finally understand what “unclean” meant, the passage stops sounding shameful and begins revealing something breathtaking about holiness, the human body, and why we desperately need Jesus.
There is a verse in Leviticus most Christians have probably never heard preached from a pulpit.
Maybe because it feels awkward.
Maybe because it raises questions we would rather not ask in church.
Maybe because the moment we read the word “unclean,” our modern minds immediately hear another word:
Dirty.
And that is where the misunderstanding begins.

Leviticus 15:18 speaks with startling directness about a man and woman having sexual intercourse involving semen and says that afterward both were to wash themselves with water and remain “unclean until evening.”
Read the Hebrew slowly:
“וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע וְרָחֲצוּ בַמַּיִם וְטָמְאוּ עַד־הָעָרֶב”
Ve’ishshah asher yishkav ish otah shikhvat-zara, verachatsu vammayim, vetam’u ad-ha‘arev.
In context, the meaning is essentially:
When a man lies with a woman in an intercourse involving semen, they are to bathe in water, and they will be ritually unclean until evening.
There it is.
No euphemistic escape.
No pretending the Bible does not talk about bodies.
No pretending God becomes embarrassed when the subject turns to sex.
But here is the question that changes everything:
If sexual intimacy between husband and wife was part of God’s good design, why could it make them “unclean”?
Was God calling marital sex sinful?
Was He saying intercourse contaminated a husband and wife?
Was sexual pleasure somehow shameful?
Was the marriage bed dirty?
No.
And confusing ritual uncleanness with moral wickedness can badly distort what Leviticus is actually teaching.
The Hebrew word appearing here comes from טָמֵא—ṭāmēʾ.
It refers in this context to ritual impurity.
That is not automatically the same thing as committing a moral sin.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because only two verses earlier, Leviticus says something similar about a man having an emission of semen.
He washes.
He remains ritually unclean until evening.
The text does not say he committed adultery.
It does not say he lusted.
It does not say he rebelled against God.
It describes a bodily condition that temporarily affected ritual status within Israel’s covenant worship system.
Move through Leviticus 15 and the pattern becomes impossible to ignore.
Discharges.
Semen.
Menstruation.
Blood.
Sexual intercourse involving semen.
Bodies doing what bodies do.
Some conditions were abnormal and required more extensive purification. Others were ordinary bodily events accompanied by temporary ritual impurity.
This is why one of the most important things you can remember when reading Leviticus is this:
“Unclean” does not automatically mean “sinful.”
A person could become ritually unclean without having committed a moral transgression.
And suddenly the scandal begins to change shape.
Because perhaps the shocking part of Leviticus 15 is not that God hated human bodies.
Perhaps it is that God cared enough about His people to teach them that approaching His holy presence was not casual.
Israel was learning to live with the presence of the Holy One in their midst.
Everything surrounding the sanctuary preached a sermon.
Clean.
Unclean.
Holy.
Common.
Approach.
Wait.
Wash.
Separate.
Return.
Again and again, Israel was being taught that God is not merely an accessory to ordinary life.
He is holy.
Human beings do not stroll casually into divine holiness on their own terms.
And yet notice something beautiful.
Leviticus 15:18 does not command a sacrifice for ordinary marital intercourse.
There is no condemnation of husband and wife for having sex simply because the temporary ritual impurity followed.
They wash.
They wait until evening.
Life continues.
That should immediately warn us against turning this passage into a declaration that marital sexuality is inherently dirty.
The rest of Scripture will not allow that interpretation anyway.
The Bible begins with God creating humanity male and female.
Before sin enters the world, God tells them to “be fruitful and multiply” in Genesis 1:28.
Genesis 2 presents husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Before the serpent.
Before the fall.
Before shame entered Eden.
Marriage and sexual union did not originate in a brothel.
They originated in the creative purpose of God.
Sin corrupted human sexuality.
Sin did not create sexuality.
That distinction matters.
Hebrews 13:4 later speaks of marriage as honorable and the marriage bed as undefiled, while simultaneously condemning sexual immorality and adultery.
So Scripture refuses both extremes.
It refuses the lie that sex itself is dirty.
And it refuses the lie that whatever we desire sexually must therefore be holy.
God created sexuality.
Therefore God—not culture, pornography, Hollywood, lust, trauma, loneliness, TikTok, our hormones, or our private fantasies—has the authority to define its boundaries.
That may be where this ancient verse suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because our generation does not suffer from a lack of information about sex.
We are drowning in it.
Images.
Videos.
Jokes.
Secret messages.
Affairs hidden behind passwords.
Pornography watched after everyone falls asleep.
Bodies compared with edited bodies.
Marriages quietly bleeding because one spouse feels unwanted.
Singles carrying memories they wish they could erase.
Believers worshiping on Sunday while fighting fantasies on Monday.
People who have confused being desired with being loved.
People who gave their bodies hoping somebody would finally stay.
People who were used.
People who used others.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who were sinned against.
People carrying shame for things they chose.
People carrying shame for things they never chose.
And somewhere beneath all that noise is a human heart whispering:
Am I dirty now?
Can God still want me?
Can Jesus really cleanse this?
That is where Leviticus becomes more than an ancient book about washing.
Because all those washings create a hunger.
Water could wash the body.
But what washes the conscience?
Waiting until evening could restore ritual status.
But what happens when the stain is inside us?
What happens when the problem is not merely something that happened to the body but something coming from the heart?
Jesus eventually put His finger directly on that wound.
In Mark 7, Christ teaches that genuine moral defilement comes from within—from the human heart—and He names things such as sexual immorality, adultery, greed, deceit, pride, and other evils.
Jesus moves the spotlight somewhere terrifying.
Inside.
That means the deepest human problem cannot be solved with soap.
You can wash your hands and still hate someone.
You can shower and still commit adultery in your imagination.
You can put on church clothes while hiding pornography on your phone.
You can sing worship songs while secretly manipulating someone sexually.
You can appear clean to everybody watching you and still know there is a locked room inside your soul that you desperately hope nobody opens.
Religion can teach you how to look clean.
Jesus came to make sinners new.
And that is where the story stops being merely about Leviticus 15.
It becomes about you.
About me.
About every person who has ever whispered:
“If people knew everything about me, would they still love me?”
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody caught you.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents never discovered it.
Maybe the browser history disappeared.
Maybe the messages were deleted.
Maybe years have passed.
Maybe everyone thinks you are the strong Christian.
But you remember.
And sometimes the enemy knows exactly which memory to replay.
That night.
That person.
That photograph.
That affair.
That addiction.
That decision.
That season.
That violation.
That secret.
And shame says:
Look at you.
Dirty.
Ruined.
Disqualified.
Unwanted.
Beyond restoration.
But shame does something the Gospel does not do.
Shame gives you an identity based upon your worst chapter.
Jesus confronts sin, but He does not need to leave the repentant sinner imprisoned inside it.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than behavior modification.
Jesus did not come merely to make dirty people behave more respectably.
He came to redeem sinners.
The cross is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that sin matters more than we wanted to admit—and the breathtaking proof that God’s mercy reaches farther than we imagined.
Jesus Christ bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The One who had no sin entered our death so sinners could receive His life.
This is where all those ancient categories begin pointing beyond themselves.
Human beings need cleansing deeper than water.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need new hearts.
We need grace.
We need Christ.
The letter to the Hebrews repeatedly contrasts the old covenant’s external regulations and ceremonial washings with the deeper cleansing accomplished through Christ.
Hebrews 9 asks how much more the blood of Christ can cleanse our conscience so that we may serve the living God.
Think about those words.
Cleanse the conscience.
Because perhaps that is where you have been bleeding.
Nobody else sees it.
But you do.
Your conscience remembers what everybody else forgot.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to wash yourself.
More church attendance.
More promises.
More resolutions.
More religious activity.
“I will never do it again.”
“This is the last time.”
“God, forgive me, and I promise…”
Then you fell again.
And eventually you stopped believing you could ever really change.
Listen carefully.
Repentance is not pretending your sin was small.
Grace is not pretending your sin was harmless.
Forgiveness is not God lowering His holiness until your behavior becomes acceptable.
The Gospel is better.
Christ took sin seriously enough to die for sinners.
And grace is powerful enough to transform the people it forgives.
Maybe you need to stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Maybe you need to stop protecting the very secret that is poisoning you.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need accountability.
Maybe you need to tell your spouse the truth.
Maybe you need to delete what keeps pulling you backward.
Maybe you need to flee rather than negotiate with temptation.
Maybe you need mature pastoral help.

Maybe wounds from sexual abuse require compassionate, trauma-informed care—and if someone sinned against you, their evil is not transformed into your moral guilt simply because you were the one wounded by it.
And maybe, beneath everything else, you need to come home to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
Because nobody gets clean enough to qualify for grace.
Grace is for people who finally realize they cannot save themselves.
This is why Leviticus 15:18 should never be weaponized to make faithful husbands and wives ashamed of marital intimacy.
The passage belongs to Israel’s ritual purity system.
It describes temporary ritual impurity following intercourse involving semen; it does not pronounce marital intercourse itself a moral transgression.
But neither should we swing to the opposite extreme and pretend the Bible has nothing serious to say about sex.
Scripture celebrates sexuality within God’s design while relentlessly confronting sexual sin.
God cares what we do with our bodies because our bodies matter.
Marriage matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Covenant matters.
Purity matters.
The person you desire is not an object.
The body on your screen belongs to a human being made in the image of God.
Your spouse is not merchandise for your appetite.
Your singleness is not permission for secret sexual slavery.
And your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
That last sentence may be the one somebody needs tonight.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Maybe somebody told you that what happened to you made you permanently dirty.
Maybe religious people knew how to expose your scandal but never showed you the road home.
Maybe you became convinced that Christianity was simply God standing over you with folded arms saying:
“Disgusting.”
But look at Jesus.
Watch how He deals with sinners who come to Him.
He tells the truth about sin.
He never needs to rename darkness as light.
Yet He receives the broken.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
He gives people futures their histories said they did not deserve.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing justice.
He rewrites the sinner’s future through redemption.
There is an enormous difference.
The Gospel does not say:
“You never sinned.”
The Gospel says there is forgiveness in Christ.
The Gospel does not say:
“Your wounds never mattered.”
The Gospel says Jesus can meet you inside them.
The Gospel does not say:
“Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus says, in effect:
Follow Me.
Come out of darkness.
Bring Me what you have been hiding.
Stop running.
Repent.
Believe.
Walk with Me.
Become new.
And perhaps that is why the words “until evening” feel unexpectedly beautiful when we read Leviticus 15 today.
The uncleanness was not forever.
Evening came.
The waiting ended.
There was a way back.
And while we should not flatten Israel’s ritual purity laws into simplistic Christian metaphors, the biblical storyline ultimately gives us something far greater than an evening sunset.
It gives us a cross.
It gives us an empty tomb.
It gives us a Savior.
There are stains water cannot touch.
But there is no repentant sinner beyond the mercy of Jesus Christ.
So if this article exposed something you have kept hidden, do not turn this moment into another five minutes of religious emotion before returning to the same chains.
Respond.
Pray.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help.
Return to Christ.
Not because commenting magically defeats temptation.
It does not.
But sometimes refusing to hide is the first crack in the wall.
If what you need most right now is prayer, simply write:
And if Jesus has already brought you through sexual brokenness, addiction, betrayal, shame, or a season you thought would destroy you, your testimony may become somebody else’s reason not to give up.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Then tell as much of your testimony as wisdom allows.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people whose only hope is a Rescuer.
Not merely because sharing helps a page grow.
Someone may be married and ashamed to ask this question.
Someone may have misunderstood Leviticus and concluded that God considers marital intimacy dirty.
Someone may be trapped in pornography.
Someone may believe sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may have been sexually wounded and still believes another person's sin made them worthless.
Put truth where shame can find it.
And if tagging someone regarding sexual struggles would embarrass or expose them, do not do that publicly. Send the article privately instead.
Love protects people even while truth confronts darkness.
Because someday someone may ask you:
“Why did Leviticus say sex made people unclean?”
And now you know the answer is far richer than:
“Because sex was dirty.”
It wasn't that simple.
Ritual impurity was not identical to moral guilt.
Marital intimacy was not thereby condemned.
The holiness laws taught Israel to distinguish categories of clean and unclean as they lived around God's sanctuary and covenant presence.
And across the unfolding biblical story, our attention is ultimately driven toward humanity's deeper problem:
Not merely bodies needing water…
but sinners needing redemption.
It cannot.
Not because sending money earns forgiveness.
It never will.
It does not.
And we will not tell you that supporting Gospel Warrior is a biblical requirement for glorifying God.
God is glorified through a life surrendered to Christ.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, discipling, and placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door before encountering it on a screen.
Every sincere share can carry biblical truth into a home we could never personally enter.
Every thoughtful comment can help another believer realize they are not fighting alone.
Every save keeps truth within reach.
Every follow keeps you connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite Christians who have grown cold.
Invite seekers.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them encounter Jesus for themselves.
If you believe work like this should continue…
If you want difficult passages explained instead of avoided…
If you want Scripture without sugarcoating, grace without compromise, conviction without hopelessness, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ…
But whether you ever give one cent or not, hear this clearly:
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).
The greatest response you could ever make to this article is not financial.
It is surrender.
Give Christ your sin.
Give Him your secret.
Give Him your sexuality.
Give Him your marriage.
Give Him your singleness.
Give Him the memories you cannot erase.
Give Him the desires you cannot control alone.
Give Him the room in your heart you keep locking whenever He gets too close.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame has been lying to you.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Offer forgiveness where Christ is calling you to release vengeance.
Seek wise help where wounds run deeper than an article can reach.
Then get up and follow Jesus.
Because perhaps the most astonishing thing hidden beneath this strange verse in Leviticus is not that two married people could become ritually unclean until evening.
It is that the God whose holiness taught Israel to wash is the same God who entered our broken world in Jesus Christ to accomplish the cleansing no basin of water could ever provide.
Your scandal may explain a chapter.
It does not have to write the ending.
Jesus still does His greatest work in lives everyone else thought were already ruined.
